meta.tier_interpretation_note: These tiers reflect modeled/measured groundwater storage trends within a Water Balance Area (WBA) over 1960–2021 relative to a reference scenario, including whether the fitted linear trend is stable/increasing or declining (and how steep the decline is). Legal standards rarely encode a specific storage-trend slope; they influence groundwater outcomes by changing pumping rules, recharge requirements, monitoring, enforcement, surface-water substitution, and water-quality constraints. Likelihood scores reflect policy-to-outcome plausibility (directness/strength of leverage), not a guarantee of any tier.

Legal Standards.name: Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) (California Water Code §10720 et seq.)
Legal Standards.note: Primary statewide framework requiring local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs) to develop and implement Groundwater Sustainability Plans (GSPs) that achieve sustainability and avoid specified “undesirable results.” SGMA is the most direct legal lever for changing pumping levels and increasing recharge, which directly affects groundwater storage trends in basins/WBAs.

key_elements.plain_definition: Local agency (or group of agencies) that manages groundwater under SGMA in a basin.
The basin plan that sets measurable objectives, projects, and rules (often including pumping limits) to reach sustainability.
Harmful conditions SGMA requires avoiding (e.g., chronic groundwater level decline, land subsidence, degraded water quality, depletion of connected surface water).
How much groundwater can be pumped long-term without causing undesirable results.
A basin the state flags for failure to form a GSA, submit/implement an adequate plan, or address chronic overdraft—triggering potential state intervention.

Legal Standards.name: State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB) SGMA backstop (probationary basin + interim plan authority)
Legal Standards.note: If local SGMA implementation fails (e.g., no adequate GSP or lack of progress), SWRCB can designate a basin probationary and adopt an interim plan, which can require pumping reporting, extraction limits, and fees—directly affecting storage trends by reducing overdraft and improving accountability.

key_elements.plain_definition: A state-imposed set of requirements for a basin when local management fails, which can include pumping restrictions and reporting.
Required measurement/estimation and reporting of how much groundwater is pumped.

Legal Standards.name: Groundwater adjudications (court decrees, watermaster administration) (judicial, basin-specific)
Legal Standards.note: In adjudicated basins, courts allocate pumping rights and impose enforceable extraction limits and monitoring. This can be a strong driver of stabilizing/increasing storage where caps are binding and compliance is enforced, but it is geographically contingent (applies only where adjudications exist).

key_elements.plain_definition: A court process that determines and limits who can pump groundwater and how much, usually with a management entity.
An entity designated to administer and enforce a court-ordered groundwater allocation (tracking pumping, collecting assessments, enforcing limits).

Legal Standards.name: Reasonable Use / Beneficial Use Doctrine (California Constitution Article X, §2 + Water Code §100)
Legal Standards.note: Foundational constraint that all water use must be reasonable and beneficial and not wasteful. For groundwater, it can support pressure toward efficiency, conservation, and (in some cases) constraints on unreasonable extraction practices—typically indirectly unless paired with specific SGMA/adjudication actions.

key_elements.plain_definition: A lawful purpose for using water (e.g., irrigation, municipal), subject to limits against waste.
Using water in a wasteful or unjustified way given conditions; can be challenged legally.

Legal Standards.name: Public Trust Doctrine (as applied in California water management; especially where groundwater pumping depletes connected surface waters)
Legal Standards.note: A legal doctrine requiring the state to consider and protect public trust resources (like fisheries, navigable waters) in water allocation decisions. Increasingly relevant where groundwater pumping depletes streamflows or harms ecosystems, potentially motivating pumping constraints or mitigation that affects storage trends—often indirect and case-specific.

key_elements.plain_definition: Natural resources the state has a duty to protect for the public (commonly linked to waterways, fisheries, recreation).
When groundwater pumping affects nearby rivers/streams (reducing flows) because the systems are physically connected.

Legal Standards.name: Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act (California Water Code §13000 et seq.) — groundwater quality regulation
Legal Standards.note: Water Boards regulate discharges that can affect groundwater quality and can require monitoring and cleanup. While this is not a direct storage-management law, groundwater quality constraints can reduce usable storage (e.g., contamination), increase treatment costs, and influence pumping/recharge strategies that interact with storage trends.

key_elements.plain_definition: Recognized uses of groundwater (e.g., drinking water, irrigation) that water-quality rules aim to protect.
Actions required to stop pollution and clean contaminated groundwater.

Legal Standards.name: Safe Drinking Water Act (federal and California implementation) — groundwater as a drinking-water source
Legal Standards.note: Drinking-water standards and regulatory requirements influence how groundwater is treated, protected, and monitored as a potable supply. This affects ‘effective storage’ (usable supply) more than physical storage, but can shift reliance toward/away from groundwater and shape recharge and blending strategies.

key_elements.plain_definition: A legal limit on how much of a contaminant can be in drinking water.
Programs and requirements intended to protect the quality of groundwater used for drinking.

Tier 1.threshold: Groundwater trend in a WBA is stable or increasing (1960–2021) AND average total storage is greater than in the reference scenario

policies.relationship: Primary legal mechanism most aligned with achieving stable/increasing trends and higher storage through pumping management + recharge projects
policies.note: Mechanism: Enforceable pumping allocations, demand management, recharge projects (spreading, banking), and requirements to avoid chronic declines can drive storage stabilization and (if aggressive) increases relative to reference.

policies.relationship: Strong leverage when state intervention occurs (typically in failing basins)
policies.note: Mechanism: Interim plan requirements (reporting, limits, fees) can force reductions in overdraft and improve management, but it is conditional on a basin entering probationary/interim status.

policies.relationship: Can directly produce stable/increasing trends where caps and compliance are strong, but only in adjudicated basins
policies.note: Mechanism: Court-ordered pumping rights/caps and watermaster enforcement can reduce extraction to (near) recharge levels and promote recharge funding—supporting Tier 1 outcomes locally.

policies.relationship: Indirect—supports ‘usable’ groundwater conditions and can shape recharge/pumping strategies
policies.note: Mechanism: Water-quality constraints can prevent practices that degrade groundwater and can require cleanup; these shape effective storage and management choices, but do not directly mandate higher physical storage.

Tier 2.threshold: Groundwater trend in a WBA is stable or increasing BUT total storage is less than in the reference scenario

policies.relationship: Direct leverage—Tier 2 can reflect partial SGMA success (stabilizing trend) without building storage above reference
policies.note: Mechanism: Pumping caps and management can stop declines (trend stabilizes) while still leaving long-term storage below reference if recharge projects are modest, lagged, or hydrology limits rebound.

policies.relationship: Direct leverage where caps stabilize trends but do not restore storage to reference levels
policies.note: Mechanism: Allocations may prevent further decline but not require enough recharge or reductions to rebuild storage above reference.

policies.relationship: Indirect—supports efficiency and reduced waste; rarely sufficient alone to produce Tier 2 outcomes
policies.note: Mechanism: Can support conservation pressure or enforcement arguments, but the main drivers of stabilizing trends are typically SGMA/adjudication rules.

Tier 3.threshold: Groundwater trend is declining, but moderately (fitted linear trend slope is less negative than -0.015 ft/yr)

policies.relationship: Direct—Tier 3 can indicate under-powered implementation, delayed projects, or partial compliance in overdrafted systems
policies.note: Mechanism: If pumping reductions/recharge projects are insufficient or phased in slowly, SGMA may reduce the rate of decline without stopping it—producing moderate negative trends.

policies.relationship: Conditional—can push a basin out of Tier 3 if activated, but only applies in failing basins
policies.note: Mechanism: State intervention can accelerate reporting and reductions; however, it is contingent on governance failure triggers and still may take time to reverse a declining trend.

policies.policy_name: Public Trust Doctrine (connected surface water impacts)
policies.relationship: Indirect—can motivate pumping constraints/mitigation where pumping harms streams, potentially reducing decline rates
policies.note: Mechanism: Legal pressure to protect public trust resources can influence decisions where groundwater pumping depletes surface waters, but translation into basin-wide storage trend changes is case-specific.

Tier 4.threshold: Groundwater trend is declining severely (slope <= -0.015 ft/yr)

policies.relationship: Direct—Tier 4 often indicates continued overdraft, delayed compliance, or inadequate controls relative to pumping demand
policies.note: Mechanism: Weak/late pumping limits, insufficient recharge capacity, or noncompliance can allow severe declines. Strengthening SGMA implementation is typically the main lever to move out of Tier 4.

policies.relationship: Direct but conditional—most relevant when local failure is severe enough to trigger state action
policies.note: Mechanism: In severe decline conditions, state intervention can impose reporting, fees, and pumping limits; effect depends on timing and enforceability and may still lag trend reversal.

policies.relationship: Potentially strong where pursued, but contingent on basin being adjudicated and decree terms being strict enough
policies.note: Mechanism: A new or strengthened adjudication can impose enforceable caps and funding for recharge/management, but it is not statewide and requires litigation/settlement and administrative capacity.

policies.policy_name: Porter-Cologne + Safe Drinking Water constraints (quality limits reduce ‘usable’ supply and may force operational shifts)
policies.relationship: Indirect—can exacerbate effective scarcity and management pressure but does not directly control storage trend slope
policies.note: Mechanism: Contamination can reduce usable supply and drive increased pumping elsewhere or higher costs; these laws shape quality protection and cleanup, not direct storage trend requirements.

Governing Agencies.name: Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs)
Governing Agencies.note: Primary local implementers of SGMA: adopt and enforce Groundwater Sustainability Plans (GSPs), set pumping allocations/fees, implement recharge and demand-management projects, and track progress toward sustainability.

Governing Agencies.name: California Department of Water Resources (DWR)
Governing Agencies.note: Reviews and evaluates GSPs for adequacy under SGMA, provides basin boundary data and technical guidance/support, and tracks statewide groundwater planning/implementation progress.

Governing Agencies.name: State Water Resources Control Board (SWRCB)
Governing Agencies.note: SGMA backstop authority: can designate probationary basins and adopt an interim plan if local SGMA implementation fails; also can require reporting/fees and enforce interim requirements.

Governing Agencies.name: California Regional Water Quality Control Boards (RWQCBs)
Governing Agencies.note: Implement Porter-Cologne regionally for groundwater quality: regulate discharges, require monitoring, and order cleanup/abatement that affect groundwater ‘usable’ conditions and management choices.

Governing Agencies.name: California Superior Courts (basin-specific) + Watermasters (where appointed)
Governing Agencies.note: In adjudicated basins, courts establish pumping rights/allocations and approve management regimes; watermasters administer, monitor, and enforce decree terms affecting extraction and (sometimes) recharge funding.

Governing Agencies.name: California Department of Public Health / State Water Resources Control Board (Drinking Water Division) + Local primacy agencies
Governing Agencies.note: Implement drinking-water regulatory programs affecting groundwater as a potable source (monitoring, compliance with contaminant limits), which influences how groundwater is used, treated, and protected as supply.
